chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
title: Royalties and writing "Back Bay Shuffle" for Artie Shaw
summary: The song sold well abroad; Shaw and McRae both signed with Robbins and agreed to split credit on songs written for him.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: How well has the song done over the years. I know, of course, that you---
-- you brought it in to the Dakota Staton session.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Yeah. The song was a big hit. It must've sold over a million by now -- probably two. Still selling.
All I know is (Inaudible) we get a lot records on it.
Foreign royalties is very big in American music.
Let's see. There are a couple of other songs that you did. There was "Back Bay Shuffle", of course, which you talked about for Artie Shaw on Traffic Jam.
I did "Back Bay" for Artie and "Traffic Jam" for Artie. They were also Jack Robbins tunes too. Artie was signed to Robbins Music and I was signed to Robbins Music.

All Artie's things went into Robbins Music. And we worked out the same agreement. If a band leader as big as Artie Shaw -- He came to me and asked me would I write some of the things that he heard in Chick Webb's
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

band, you know, when we went to Boston. So I agreed to write with him. We're going to split the thing down. Because Artie Shaw was very big and we were going to write a lot of things together. So -- I say, "Okay, I'll give you half of the tune (Unaudible), you gonna make the song anyway," you know. So we just cut -- like cut in on a song. (Unaudible) you got a third or you got a half. It's always cut in with the name that's going to be on the song which would make big selling power, you know. So, that's the way it worked out with Artie.
